children: By Emily Ou Yong
Iron ore futures fell to their lowest level since August 24 on Monday, as steel mill profitability tumbled to a historic low.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
traded 1.39% lower at 710 yuan ($105.86) a metric ton, as of 0315 GMT.
The benchmark October iron ore <SZZFV6> on the Singapore Exchange was 0.49% lower at $96.05 a metric ton.
Steel mill profitability fell 22.51 percentage points week-on-week to 7.79%, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.
Steel mill losses widened significantly, with the loss range deepening to a historic low, analysts at Chinese broker Everbright Futures said in a note.
The blast furnace ironmaking capacity utilisation rate of 247 surveyed steel mills was 88.73%, down 0.19 percentage points from the previous week, Mysteel data showed.

Domestic steel demand weakened further in the third quarter, with construction steel demand continuing to soften and fixed asset investment declining further month-on-month in July, broker Galaxy Futures said in a note.

Overseas steel demand remained resilient but is showing signs of a delayed pickup, the analysts said, adding that domestic end-user demand is unlikely to improve meaningfully in September, leaving the outlook for iron ore prices generally bearish.
Losses were limited, however, by continued destocking at Chinese ports.
Iron ore inventory at major Chinese ports fell 0.88% week-on-week to 151.29 million metric tons last week, data from consultancy Steelhome showed.

Steel mills' imported iron ore inventories rose 1.41 million metric tons to 90.44 million metric tons last week, Mysteel data showed, pointing to early signs of restocking even as port stocks decline.
Other steelmaking ingredients on the DCE fell, with coking coal
NYMEX:ACT1!
and coke (DCJcv1) down 1.33% and 1.6%, respectively.
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were broadly weaker. Rebar
fell 0.71%, hot-rolled coil
lost 0.87% and stainless steel
edged 0.48% lower, while wire rod (SWRcv1) was flat.
($1 = 6.7068 Chinese yuan)
